rows.question: What does a CI project key start with, and how do you store it?
rows.output:
A CI project key starts with `l10p_`. An owner or admin creates it on the project's page under **CI keys**, and it's shown once.

Store it in your CI's secrets, never in a file you commit. Send it as `Authorization: Bearer` to the registry API. Latitude 10 keeps only a SHA-256 hash of the key, so a lost key can't be shown again. Revoke it on the same page and create a new one.

- Key format and storage: https://docs.latitude10.tech/get-started/keys-and-tokens
- Registry API authentication: https://docs.latitude10.tech/registry-api

For help with setup, contact https://latitude10.tech/contact or jorge@latitude10.tech.

rows.question: How do I rotate a CI key?
rows.output:
To rotate a CI key, you create a new one, switch your CI to it, then revoke the old one. The docs don't describe a single rotate step, so these steps use the documented create and revoke actions:

- Open your project's page and go to **CI keys**. Only an owner or admin can create or revoke keys.
- Create a new project key. It starts with `l10p_` and is shown once, so copy it right away.
- Replace the old key in your CI's secrets. Never commit it to a file.
- Revoke the old key on the same page. It stops working at once, so update CI first to avoid failed pushes.

Keys are stored only as hashes, so a lost key can't be shown again. Revoke it and create another. Details: https://docs.latitude10.tech/get-started/keys-and-tokens and https://docs.latitude10.tech/registry-api

rows.question: Which hosts are refused as a hosted MCP base URL?
rows.output:
A hosted MCP base URL is refused if it is:

- Longer than the limit (the message is "Use a shorter URL.")
- Not https, or doesn't parse
- Contains a user name or password (store the credential instead)
- Contains a port (only the default https port is allowed)
- Contains a query or fragment (each tool adds its own)
- An IP address in any spelling, a single-label name, or a private name (localhost, local, internal, localdomain, lan, arpa, test, invalid, example, onion)
- latitude10.tech or Cloudflare's own names

The check runs before anything is fetched, and the messages never repeat the URL. Full list: https://docs.latitude10.tech/hosted-mcp/refused-hosts

For other questions, see /contact or jorge@latitude10.tech.

rows.question: Which Python version does the generated Python SDK need, and what does it depend on?
rows.output:
The generated Python SDK needs Python 3.11 or newer (`requires-python = ">=3.11"` in its `pyproject.toml`). Its one runtime dependency is `httpx`.

The package has a sync and an async client and type hints throughout. Details are at https://docs.latitude10.tech/sdks/python.

rows.question: Does the generated Python SDK retry when it gets a 429?
rows.output:
Yes. The Python SDK retries a `429` with backoff, and it honours the `Retry-After` header.

It also retries connection errors, timeouts, `408` and `5xx`. `POST` and `PATCH` are retried only when an idempotency key is set, either with `idempotency_key=` on a call or from an operation's `Idempotency-Key` header. You can set `max_retries` and `timeout` on the client or per call.

If the retries run out, you get an `APIError` with the status code, headers, body and request ID.

Details: https://docs.latitude10.tech/sdks/python

rows.question: How do I serve my docs on my own domain?
rows.output:
You can serve your docs on a subdomain you own, such as `docs.example.com`, on the Pro plan and up. The certificate is issued and renewed for you.

- In your project's Overview, open **Docs** and add the subdomain.
- At your DNS provider, add a CNAME: `docs.example.com CNAME domains.latitude10.tech`.
- Choose **Check now**. The domain goes live once its hostname and certificate are active.

Apex domains such as `example.com` aren't supported yet, and a latitude10.tech name can't be used. The number of custom domains depends on your plan.

Full guide: https://docs.latitude10.tech/docs-hosting/custom-domains

For help with your setup, write to https://latitude10.tech/contact or jorge@latitude10.tech.

rows.question: Is changing an operationId a breaking change?
rows.output:
In Latitude 10's registry, changing an operationId is a warning, not a breaking change. The diff flags `operation-id-changed` because agents will see a new tool name.

It does affect SDKs, though. A changed operationId counts as a renamed method, so the next SDK package gets a major version bump.

- Registry diff: https://docs.latitude10.tech/registry/breaking-changes
- SDK versioning: https://docs.latitude10.tech/sdks/versioning

If you want the diff to fail your CI, set `fail-on-breaking` in the GitHub Action. It only fails on breaking changes, so an operationId change won't stop the build.

rows.question: Does Latitude 10's SSO support SAML?
rows.output:
No. Latitude 10's SSO is OpenID Connect only, using the authorization code flow with PKCE and a nonce. There's no SAML. It has been tested end to end with Okta.

- SSO is included with Business and Enterprise. Business allows 1 connection and 5 email domains per workspace. Enterprise limits are set by contract.
- Owners can require SSO for the workspace, with break-glass access if the provider is down.

Details: https://docs.latitude10.tech/enterprise/sso

If you need SAML, ask us whether it fits your setup at https://latitude10.tech/contact or jorge@latitude10.tech.

rows.question: What callback URL do I register with my identity provider for workspace SSO?
rows.output:
Register this callback URL in your identity provider's OpenID Connect web app:

- https://latitude10.tech/api/workspace/auth/sso/callback

SSO is OpenID Connect only (authorization code flow with PKCE and a nonce), with no SAML. It's available on Business and Enterprise. After you register the app, the workspace owner enters the issuer URL, client ID and secret on the workspace's SSO settings page. Your email domain must also be proved with a DNS TXT record.

Full setup guide: https://docs.latitude10.tech/enterprise/sso

For help with your provider, contact https://latitude10.tech/contact or jorge@latitude10.tech.

rows.question: What files does a published docs site serve for AI agents?
rows.output:
A published docs site serves these files for agents, all built at push time:

- /llms.txt: every page in the navigation, with its title, Markdown address and description
- /llms-full.txt: every page's Markdown in one file, in navigation order
- /<page>.md: any page as Markdown. Sending `Accept: text/markdown` to the page's own address gets the same
- /skill.md: an agent skill describing the site (you can supply your own)
- /reference.md: the API reference as Markdown, once it's published
- /mcp: a read-only docs MCP server with search_docs, read_page and list_pages. It needs no key, but has a daily call limit per site
- /mcp/server-card and /.well-known/mcp: the MCP server card
- /.well-known/ai-catalog.json: an AI Catalog pointing at that card

Every site gets these with nothing to set up. Details: https://docs.latitude10.tech/docs-hosting/agent-files

rows.question: Can people sign in to my hosted MCP server with my own identity provider instead of a key?
rows.output:
Yes. On Pro and up, people can sign in to a hosted MCP server through your own OpenID Connect provider instead of using a key.

- Register an OpenID Connect app with your provider, using the callback URL shown on your project's MCP page.
- Enter the issuer, client ID and secret on that page. The secret is stored and never shown again.
- Choose keys only, sign-in only, or both, so agents with keys and signed-in people can use the server side by side.

Each server gets its own authorization server, and its tokens work only for that server. They are never sent to your API. Your API still gets the stored credential, or each person's own provider token if you choose.

Access can follow your provider's groups through claim rules, and owners or admins can revoke any client.

Full details: https://docs.latitude10.tech/hosted-mcp/oauth. Plans: /pricing. Questions: https://latitude10.tech/contact or jorge@latitude10.tech.

rows.question: What will the API client's proxy call?
rows.output:
The API client's proxy makes one request to the API you specify, and only to a host you have verified for that project. The request is built from the envelope the browser sends, nothing else:

- https only, on the default port, to a verified public host
- GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD or OPTIONS, with a body of up to 256 KB
- No cookies, Origin or Referer, and no Host or forwarding headers
- Sent once, never retried or redirected, cut off after 15 seconds, with the answer read up to 1 MB

The answer comes back as JSON with the status, headers (without Set-Cookie), body and timing. The proxy is available on Pro and up. Details: https://docs.latitude10.tech/api-client/direct-and-proxy

rows.question: What does the readiness check look at?
rows.output:
The readiness check scores an OpenAPI 3.0 or 3.1 spec from 0 to 100 for how well AI agents will use it. It looks at:

- operationIds, summaries and descriptions
- parameters, enums and examples
- JSON bodies, response and error schemas
- pagination, auth and idempotency
- the number of tools

It then says what to fix first. The rules are open source (MIT) in the openapi-agent-check CLI at https://github.com/jorgeortega/openapi-agent-check. The check is free in your browser, as an MCP tool, and from the CLI. Full docs: https://latitude10.tech/agent-readiness
